title: The tax collector's table (Matthew 9:9–13)
hook: Matthew is called from his booth and throws a dinner full of the wrong people

segments.voice: Yesterday, four friends went through the roof. Your line was friends dig through roofs. Whose mat did you lift? Day thirty-seven.

Think of the least popular job in your town. The person who tows your car. The one who sends the final notice. Now make it worse: this person works for the occupying power, and everyone assumes they skim a little extra for themselves. That was a tax collector in Galilee. In Capernaum there was a toll booth, and in it sat a man named Matthew. People crossed the street to avoid him. Pious people wouldn't eat with him. And one day Jesus walks past the booth, stops, looks at him, and says two words. Today: the man at the booth, and the dinner that followed.
screen: `THE LEAST POPULAR JOB IN TOWN.` → `MATTHEW AT HIS BOOTH.` → `TWO WORDS.`

segments.voice: The two words are: "Follow me." And the Gospel that carries his name says simply: "And he arose up and followed him." No speech. No list of conditions. He gets up from the money and goes. Mark and Luke tell the same story and call him Levi. Then comes the dinner. Jesus sits at table in the house, and many tax collectors and sinners come and eat with him and his disciples. Matthew has invited everyone he knows, and everyone he knows is the wrong crowd. Some Pharisees, who took holiness very seriously, ask the disciples: why does your master eat with tax collectors and sinners? In that world, sharing a table meant sharing a life. Jesus hears it and answers with a picture from medicine: "They that are in health need not a physician, but they that are ill." Then he sends them to the prophet Hosea: "I will have mercy and not sacrifice." A doctor who avoids sick people isn't much of a doctor. He came for the ones who know they need help. Catholics keep Matthew's feast on September twenty-first. In Rome there's a famous Caravaggio painting of this moment: a beam of light across a dark counting table, and a man pointing at himself, as if to say, me? And Pope Francis took his motto from an old homily by Saint Bede about this scene. In Latin: miserando atque eligendo. Roughly, by having mercy, and by choosing. He looked at Matthew with mercy, and chose him.
screen: `FOLLOW ME. HE AROSE AND FOLLOWED.` · `A DINNER FULL OF THE WRONG PEOPLE.` · `A DOCTOR FOR THE SICK.` · `BY HAVING MERCY, AND BY CHOOSING.` · then, large: `I WILL HAVE MERCY AND NOT SACRIFICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle and breathe. Think of someone outside your usual circle. Someone you wouldn't normally sit with at lunch. The coworker nobody talks to. The neighbor you nod at. The relative the family whispers about. Picture sitting across a table from them. Notice what rises in you: awkwardness, judgment, maybe curiosity. Then picture the look Jesus gave Matthew, and imagine being looked at that way yourself. If you pray, you can ask for that look. The bell holds the time.
The tax collector's table. Matthew called from his booth, and a dinner full of people nobody else would eat with. Today's word.
Your line: he came for the sick. Sometime this week, eat with someone outside your circle, even a coffee, even ten minutes. Day thirty-seven.

screen: `DAY 37 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE WOMAN AT THE WELL.`

howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Matthew, apostle and evangelist, on September 21, when this Gospel is read at Mass; Pope Francis's episcopal motto, miserando atque eligendo, comes from Saint Bede's homily on it.

fork.setup: you're Matthew. a teacher has just called you from your booth, and you've followed him. what do you do next?
options: keep it quiet so your old life doesn't embarrass him.
throw a dinner and invite all your friends, the wrong crowd included.
go to the synagogue to make amends first.
fork.reveal: many tax collectors and sinners sit down to eat with Jesus. when questioned, he says the sick are the ones who need a doctor.

original.note: Greek: a toll or tax collector, the job Matthew left. The old English Bibles say publican.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus picks a tax collector to be one of the twelve.
what it means: he calls a man everyone avoided, then eats with his friends, and says he came for the sick.
what a scholar hears: Bede's homily, miserando atque eligendo, by having mercy and by choosing, now the motto of Pope Francis.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of Matthew 9:9, 9:12, 9:13 given from memory; confirm. 'Follow me' is also from 9:9.
Tax collectors in Capernaum likely collected tolls for Herod Antipas rather than directly for Rome; the script says 'works for the occupying power'. Confirm or soften to 'works for the rulers'.
Pharisees presented neutrally ('who took holiness very seriously'); confirm this is fair.
Caravaggio, The Calling of Saint Matthew (1599–1600), Contarelli Chapel, San Luigi dei Francesi, Rome. Who in the painting is Matthew is debated; the script says 'a man pointing at himself'. Confirm.
Pope Francis's motto from Bede, Homily 21 (Office of Readings, September 21). Confirm homily number.
Matthew's authorship of the Gospel is traditional ('the Gospel that carries his name'); confirm phrasing.
